overview.title: GradientTape in the training step, and the full training loop
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.5 Looking back at our first example
overview.main_topic: A minimal GradientTape example (gradient of y = 2x + 3), one_training_step rewritten with GradientTape, the from-scratch fit() function looping over epochs and batches, and the start of a test drive on MNIST
overview.central_idea: With GradientTape recording the forward pass, the training step becomes complete: predictions, per-sample loss and average loss are computed inside the tape scope, tape.gradient(average_loss, model.weights) returns one gradient per weight, and update_weights applies them. An epoch is the training step repeated for every batch, and fit() is the epoch repeated epochs times.
overview.importance: This page closes the loop: the from-scratch model can now be trained exactly like keras's fit on p.76. It shows the minimal skeleton of any training loop (nested loops over epochs and batches around a gradient step), which the book generalizes in chapter 7.
learning_objectives: Use tf.GradientTape to compute the derivative of a simple function and interpret the result (dy/dx = 2 for y = 2x + 3).
Explain which lines of one_training_step must be inside the tape scope and why.
Explain why tape.gradient is called on average_loss (a scalar) with respect to model.weights.
Read the fit() function: outer loop over epochs, a fresh BatchGenerator per epoch, inner loop over num_batches, periodic loss logging.
Prepare MNIST inputs by reshaping (60000, 28, 28) to (60000, 784).

summary:
The page finishes the GradientTape demonstration begun on p.80. Inside `with tf.GradientTape() as tape:` (callout: *opens a GradientTape scope*) the code computes `y = 2 * x + 3` (*applies some tensor operations to our variable*), then `grad_of_y_wrt_x = tape.gradient(y, x)` *uses the tape to retrieve the gradient of the output y with respect to our variable x*. For this affine function the gradient is 2 everywhere, in particular at x = 0.

**Rewritten training step.** `one_training_step()` is rewritten with the tape, which removes the need for a separate `get_gradients_of_loss_wrt_weights()`. The forward pass (`predictions = model(images_batch)`), the per-sample `ops.sparse_categorical_crossentropy` and `average_loss = ops.mean(loss)` run inside the tape scope; then `gradients = tape.gradient(average_loss, model.weights)` gives one gradient per weight, `update_weights(gradients, model.weights)` applies them, and the function returns `average_loss`. Unlike listing 2.9 on p.79, the gradient is taken of the scalar average loss.

**Section 2.5.3, The full training loop.** An epoch is the repetition of the training step for each batch in the training data, and the full loop is the repetition of the epoch. The from-scratch `fit(model, images, labels, epochs, batch_size=128)` prints the epoch number, creates a new `BatchGenerator(images, labels)`, loops `num_batches` times calling `batch_generator.next()` and `one_training_step`, and prints the loss every 100 batches (`f"loss at batch {batch_counter}: {loss:.2f}"`).

**Test drive.** The page begins running it: load MNIST with `mnist.load_data()` and reshape the training images to `(60000, 28 * 28)`; the rest (type conversion, the call to `fit`, evaluation) continues on p.82.

concepts.name: tf.GradientTape
concepts.definition: TensorFlow scope that records operations so the gradient of a scalar output with respect to inputs can be retrieved with tape.gradient.
concepts.intuition: Record the forward computation, then replay it backward.
concepts.technical: with tf.GradientTape() as tape: y = f(x); tape.gradient(y, x).
concepts.significance: Provides get_gradients_of_loss_wrt_weights for the from-scratch model.
concepts.misconception: Gradients can only be taken of operations executed inside the scope; computing the loss outside the with-block gives no gradient.

concepts.name: Training step (complete)
concepts.definition: Forward pass and loss recorded on a tape, gradient of the average loss with respect to model.weights, weight update.
concepts.technical: gradients = tape.gradient(average_loss, model.weights); update_weights(gradients, model.weights); return average_loss.
concepts.example: One call on a (128, 784) batch changes all 407,050 weights by tiny amounts.
concepts.misconception: Returning average_loss does not affect training; it is only for monitoring.

concepts.name: Training loop (fit from scratch)
concepts.definition: An outer loop over epochs and an inner loop over batches, calling the training step for each batch.
concepts.intuition: Do the per-batch step for the whole dataset, then do that again several times.
concepts.technical: for epoch in range(epochs): gen = BatchGenerator(...); for i in range(gen.num_batches): one_training_step(model, *gen.next()).
concepts.significance: What Keras's fit does under the hood (p.76, p.239).
concepts.example: epochs=5 with 469 batches per epoch -> 2,345 training steps.
concepts.misconception: The fit here does not report accuracy or validation loss; it only prints training loss every 100 batches.

concepts.name: Epoch
concepts.definition: Repetition of the training step for each batch in the training data.
concepts.intuition: One full lap through the dataset.
concepts.technical: Implemented by the inner loop over batch_generator.num_batches.
concepts.significance: Unit of the outer loop in fit.
concepts.example: 469 steps per epoch for MNIST with batch size 128.
concepts.misconception: An epoch is not a fixed number of steps; it depends on dataset size and batch size.

code.title: Gradient of y = 2x + 3 with GradientTape
code.original_code:
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    y = 2 * x + 3
grad_of_y_wrt_x = tape.gradient(y, x)
code.what_it_does: Records the computation y = 2x + 3 and asks the tape for dy/dx.

line_explanations.explanation: Callout: inside the scope, applies some tensor operations to our variable.
Callout: uses the tape to retrieve the gradient of the output y with respect to our variable x. Called after the scope closes.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: x (scalar, from p.80). Output: grad_of_y_wrt_x, expected value 2.
code.algorithm: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation over two recorded operations.
code.theory_link: Derivative as slope (p.65) and chain rule (p.71), automated.
pitfalls: Beyond the book: x was created with tf.zeros, a constant; TensorFlow only watches trainable tf.Variable objects automatically, so without tape.watch(x) (or x = tf.Variable(0.)) tape.gradient returns None.
By default a tape can be used for only one gradient call (unless persistent=True).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: a version that returns 2.0
x = tf.Variable(0.0)
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    y = 2 * x + 3
print(tape.gradient(y, x))  # tf.Tensor(2.0, ...)

code.title: one_training_step rewritten with GradientTape
code.original_code:
def one_training_step(model, images_batch, labels_batch):
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        predictions = model(images_batch)
        loss = ops.sparse_categorical_crossentropy(labels_batch, predictions)
        average_loss = ops.mean(loss)
    gradients = tape.gradient(average_loss, model.weights)
    update_weights(gradients, model.weights)
    return average_loss
code.what_it_does: A complete training step: forward pass and loss recorded on a tape, gradients of the average loss with respect to all weights, weight update, and return of the batch's average loss.

line_explanations.explanation: Forward pass through the two NaiveDense layers.
Per-sample crossentropy, then its mean: the scalar to minimize.
After leaving the scope, differentiate average_loss with respect to [W1, b1, W2, b2].
Apply the update (hand-written SGD or optimizers.SGD from p.80).
Return the scalar loss for logging.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: model, images_batch (128, 784), labels_batch (128,). Effect: weights updated. Returns: scalar average loss.
code.theory_link: Steps 2-5 of mini-batch SGD (p.68); backpropagation (p.70-p.74) done by the tape.
pitfalls: update_weights must be called outside or after the gradient computation; updating before tape.gradient would mismatch the recorded graph.
This version uses the TensorFlow backend; with JAX or PyTorch the gradient mechanism differs (chapter 3).

deeper.title: From-scratch fit vs keras fit
deeper.body:
| | This page | `model.fit` (p.76) |
|---|---|---|
| Batching | `BatchGenerator`, fixed order | built in, shuffled by default |
| Gradients | `tf.GradientTape` | backend autodiff |
| Update | `update_weights` (SGD, lr 1e-3) | `optimizer="adam"` |
| Logging | loss every 100 batches | loss and metrics per epoch, progress bar |
| Steps for 5 epochs | 5 x 469 = 2,345 | 2,345 |

Note that the optimizers differ (SGD here, Adam in the first example), so the loss curves will not be identical. (Comparison compiled for these notes.)

deeper.title: Why the loss must be computed inside the tape
deeper.body:
1. The tape only knows about operations executed while it is active.
2. `average_loss` depends on the weights through `model(images_batch)` and the crossentropy.
3. If those operations ran before `with tf.GradientTape()`, the tape would see no path from the weights to the loss, and `tape.gradient` would return `None` for each weight.
4. The update call is placed outside the scope because it does not need to be differentiated.

takeaways: GradientTape records operations in its scope; tape.gradient(y, x) returns dy/dx (2 for y = 2x + 3).
The complete training step records forward pass and loss on the tape, differentiates the scalar average loss with respect to model.weights, then updates the weights.
An epoch is the training step repeated over all batches; fit repeats the epoch epochs times, here with a fresh BatchGenerator each epoch.
With 5 epochs, the from-scratch fit performs the same 2,345 updates as Keras's fit.
Inputs must be reshaped to (60000, 784) before training.

questions.question: If the tape example used y = 5 * x * x + 3 instead, what would tape.gradient(y, x) return at x = 0 and at x = 2?

questions.question: In the rewritten one_training_step, which value is differentiated?
options: average_loss, the scalar mean over the batch
questions.answer: average_loss, the scalar mean over the batch
questions.explanation: The code calls tape.gradient(average_loss, model.weights). The per-sample loss is an intermediate, predictions are model outputs, and labels are constants.

questions.question: Why are the forward pass and the loss computation placed inside the with tf.GradientTape() block while update_weights is outside?
questions.answer: The tape must record the operations that connect the weights to the loss in order to differentiate it; the update itself does not need to be differentiated and happens after the gradients are obtained.
questions.explanation: GradientTape records the tensor operations run inside it (p.80); tape.gradient replays them backward.

questions.question: How many times is the loss printed per epoch for MNIST with batch size 128, and at which batches?
questions.explanation: num_batches = 469 (batch_counter 0-468), and the print happens when batch_counter % 100 == 0.

questions.question: Why does fit create a new BatchGenerator at the beginning of every epoch?
options: Because BatchGenerator's index only increases, so a new one restarts from the first sample
To change the batch size each epoch
questions.answer: Because BatchGenerator's index only increases, so a new one restarts from the first sample
questions.explanation: BatchGenerator (p.79) starts at index 0 and only advances. It does not shuffle, the batch size is always the default, and weights are untouched by it.

questions.question: Compare the from-scratch fit with model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=5, batch_size=128) from p.76. What is the same and what is different?
questions.answer: Same: nested loops of 5 epochs x 469 batches of 128, forward pass, sparse categorical crossentropy, gradients by autodiff, one update per batch. Different: SGD with lr 1e-3 instead of Adam, no shuffling, no accuracy metric, simpler logging.
questions.explanation: The page's definition of an epoch and full loop matches p.76; the differences come from the hand-written update (p.80) and BatchGenerator (p.79).

questions.question: What shape does train_images have before and after the reshape in the test drive?
questions.explanation: reshape((60000, 28 * 28)) flattens each 28x28 image into a 784-vector, matching the first NaiveDense's input_size.

questions.answer: Layers and model = keras.Sequential; update_weights = optimizer; one_training_step = one iteration inside fit; fit = epochs x batches loop.
